claim: To win, DOJ must show Apple has monopoly power (ability to control prices/exclude competition) AND that power was willfully maintained through anticompetitive conduct, not superior products.
stance_target: legal standard for DOJ v. Apple
scope_conditions: Section 2 Sherman Act, Grinnell two-element test
quoted_support: the DOJ will need to show that Apple has obtained monopoly power...using anticompetitive practices, rather than simply outcompeting rivals on the merits.

claim: The DOJ's proposed US performance-smartphone submarket gives Apple over 70% share; the broader US smartphone market gives Apple 65% share by revenue, but Apple's global market share is only ~23%.
stance_target: market definition dispute determinative of monopoly finding
scope_conditions: DOJ complaint figures, March 2024; global figure from Counterpoint Research
quoted_support: the DOJ cites Apple's estimated market share of over 70 percent of U.S. sales...Apple still has a 65 percent share by revenue in that broader market...Apple smartphones only have 23 percent of market share [globally].

claim: Fewer than 10% of smartphone purchasers are first-time buyers, meaning rivals must convert existing iPhone users rather than capture new entrants — a structural durability factor for Apple's installed base.
quoted_support: the DOJ asserts fewer than 10 percent of smartphone purchasers are buying their first smartphone, meaning that for rivals to gain new customers, they must usually convince current iPhone users to switch.

claim: Under existing case law, a firm generally has no affirmative antitrust duty to deal with rivals except in narrow circumstances lacking any efficiency justification.
stance_target: Apple's legal defense (though later rejected at pleading stage by the D.N.J. court)
scope_conditions: Aspen Skiing/Trinko line of Supreme Court precedent
quoted_support: Apple has no affirmative duty to deal with rivals...Only in extreme cases where no efficiency justifications support the practice has the Supreme Court found a refusal to deal anticompetitive.
